title: 2 Kings 10:32–36
context: In Jehu’s days the LORD begins to cut away Israel’s territory. Hazael of Syria strikes the land east of the Jordan, the regions of Gad, Reuben, and Manasseh, from Aroer by the Arnon through Gilead and Bashan. The account of Jehu closes with the standard reference to the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel, his burial in Samaria, the accession of his son Jehoahaz, and a reign of twenty-eight years.

verses.text: In those days the LORD began to cut away parts of Israel; and Hazael struck them in all the borders of Israel
verses.arminianNotes: In those days the LORD began to cut away parts of Israel, and Hazael struck its borders. Arminian readers note that the narrator connects Israel’s losses to the LORD, following directly after the report of Jehu’s failures.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s discipline on Israel through a foreign king, as Elisha had foreseen with grief (8:12). Both traditions read the verse as showing that Jehu’s incomplete reform was followed by national decline.

verses.text: from the Jordan eastward, all the land of Gilead, the Gadites, and the Reubenites, and the Manassites, from Aroer, which is by the valley of the Arnon, even Gilead and Bashan.
verses.arminianNotes: Hazael strikes the land east of the Jordan, from Aroer by the Arnon through Gilead and Bashan. Arminian readers note the extent of the losses, covering the territory of Gad, Reuben, and part of Manasseh.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the loss of land as a sign of covenant discipline. Shared ground: the exact location of Aroer is debated, though it is generally placed near the Arnon, and the verse describes the broad scope of Israel’s losses.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Jehu, and all that he did, and all his might, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of Jehu’s acts are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel. Arminian readers note the standard formula, which points to a source no longer available to readers today.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the narrator’s selective focus as interested chiefly in Jehu’s relation to the LORD rather than in all his achievements. Both traditions read the verse as a regular closing formula for a king’s reign.

verses.text: Jehu slept with his fathers; and they buried him in Samaria. Jehoahaz his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu dies, is buried in Samaria, and his son Jehoahaz reigns. Arminian readers note that the dynasty continues, as the LORD promised in 10:30, despite Jehu’s failure to walk fully in his law.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God keeping his word to Jehu even as Israel faces decline. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the start of the promised four generations of Jehu’s line on the throne.

verses.text: The time that Jehu reigned over Israel in Samaria was twenty-eight years.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu reigned over Israel in Samaria twenty-eight years. Arminian readers note the length of his reign, a long period marked by both the removal of Baal and the continuation of Jeroboam’s sins.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the summary as closing a reign that was used by God yet fell short of wholehearted faithfulness. Both traditions read the closing notice as completing an account that holds achievement and failure together.
